The benchmarked 1.1.x line sits on ed25519-dalek 1.0.1, affected by RUSTSEC-2022-0093 / CVE-2022-50237 (double public key signing oracle); the 'serialized' row exercises exactly that Ed25519Keypair.from_bytes(64-byte) path, so do not use 1.1.x. The February 2023 bench loop never called .free() (about three leaked boxed objects per iteration); the deimos benchSync harness has no warm-up and averages all 1,000 performance.now() samples; its summary prints slowdowns as '0.67x faster' and '0.54x faster'. Baseline @noble/curves 0.7.x (early 2023) is old; the same table shows berith slower than supercop.wasm 5.0.1 (187.96 vs 281.68 us) and node:crypto (152.67 us), so the win is only against pure JS. Each iteration bundles keygen, sign and verify. Unlicense (no patent grant).

tier_reason: Enricher: README plots were produced by commit 2796c53 (2021-11-15) on a Vector Class Library build, not the EVE code the README now credits; scalar per-element-division baselines and no NumPy harness. First-party plots, C stays with corrected provenance.

corrections.caveats: README gives methodology and CPU but no compiler, flags or numeric table; the four PNG plots are the only results and the figures are approximate readings of log-scale axes. Provenance: the plots were committed on 2021-11-15 (commit 2796c53) when vstat was built on the Vector Class Library with hard-coded Vec8f/Vec4d types; the README now credits EVE for the same unchanged plots, and the 2026 EVE code (width set by compile flags, no -march in the presets) has no published numbers. The 50-130x over GSL and 14-40x over Boost.Accumulators compare a vectorised one-pass accumulator against scalar code doing per-element divisions (GSL in long double over two passes, Boost with two fdiv per sample); linasm's timing includes its extra mean passes; no NumPy harness exists in test/ at the plot commit or at HEAD; MKL was not used. The benchmark adds results to a local double never passed to nanobench's doNotOptimizeAway. The float accumulator saturates at 2^24 elements per lane. The Python binding computes float64 arrays as accumulate<float>. vstat ties linasm on double variance and is about 1.2-1.4x faster on the other three plots. README says C++17 but CMakeLists.txt requires C++20.

tier_reason: Enricher: the measured ChainSafe/bls commit f4f1739 is recoverable (Node 12.x, bls-eth-wasm ^0.4.4, @chainsafe/blst ^0.1.3, noble-bls12-381 ^0.7.2) and its pre-hashing and wrapper subgroup-check asymmetries understate herumi's lead; independent third-party run, B stays with corrected caveats.

corrections.caveats: Third-party numbers from ChainSafe/bls commit f4f1739 (2020-12-07 table, CI run 1513710175 now 404): Node 12.x on ubuntu-latest, bls-eth-wasm ^0.4.4 (Emscripten build), @chainsafe/blst ^0.1.3 and noble-bls12-381 ^0.7.2; the CPU is not recoverable. Harness asymmetries mostly favour the baseline: noble's verify, verifyAggregate, verifyMultiple and sign rows received messages already hashed to G2 (hash-to-curve excluded from noble's timing, included in herumi's), and ChainSafe's Signature constructor calls isValidOrder(), so herumi's sign and aggregate-signatures rows include a G2 subgroup check noble skips; only warm-up cuts the other way (noble 10 runs, herumi and blst 100, plain means, no warm-up). runForAllImplementations does not await its async callback. herumi has since reported about 1.1x (2022), 10% and 4% (2024) speedups and switched from Emscripten to clang in v1.5.0; noble-bls12-381 is deprecated in favour of @noble/curves, so both sides are stale. Not compared with herumi's own library compiled natively (blst native, 5-10x faster, is a different library). wasm is single-threaded with a fixed 1 MiB stack; messages must be 32 bytes. No LICENSE file: README says 'modified new BSD License', package.json BSD-3-Clause.

tier_reason: Enricher: example harness asymmetries (ispc vector math library vs scalar libm, -m64-only C++ reference, 128k identical options, printed-average checks) and the disagreement between the paper's clang baseline and the perf page's gcc baseline; peer-reviewed InPar 2012 paper, B stays with corrected caveats.

corrections.caveats: Evidence is from ISPC's Intel authors: a peer-reviewed paper (InPar 2012) plus Intel's perf page, both measured around 2011-2012 on first-generation AVX and SSE4 hardware with an unnamed Core i7 model, unstated flags and an unstated ispc version; nothing newer is published. The baseline is serial non-SIMD C++, not hand-written intrinsics or SIMD libraries (Highway, xsimd); the paper gives only user anecdotes for intrinsics parity (0.99x-1.05x). Harness asymmetries in the examples behind the numbers: the serial C++ references call scalar libm expf/logf/powf while the ispc kernels use ispc's own vectorized math library, so the options-pricing speedups mix SIMD with a math-library swap; the examples' CMake builds the C++ reference with -m64 and Release defaults only (no -march), on Windows with /fp:fast /Oi; the options example prices 128k identical options (no lane divergence) and checks results only by printed averages; each example reports the minimum of 3 rdtsc-timed runs. The two Intel tables on the same iMac disagree more than the paper's 'gcc gave essentially the same results' admits: Binomial 7.94x (perf page, gcc 4.2.1) vs 4.39x (paper, clang), Ray Tracer 4.31x vs 6.85x, and Black-Scholes reaches 8.45x on one core with 8-wide AVX. Multi-core figures fold in tasks and hyper-threading (243.18x on 40 cores exceeds the 160x ideal). ispc is a compiler for an SPMD C dialect, not an intrinsics library, so the category fit is loose.
